title: Serverless Trade-offs: When Not to Use It
summary: The honest cost, latency, and lock-in trade-offs that decide whether serverless fits a given workload — and the shapes of workload it fits badly.

slides.markdown:
Serverless is a genuine win for the right shape of workload — and a genuine loss for the wrong one. The honest trade-offs — cost crossover, vendor lock-in, debugging difficulty — are exactly what separates a good serverless decision from a fashionable one.

- The question isn't "is serverless good" — it's "is *this workload's* traffic pattern one it's good at."
- Every trade-off below has a concrete, calculable threshold, not just a vibe.

| Traffic pattern | On-demand VM/container | Serverless (pay-per-invocation) |
|---|---|---|
| Low volume, spiky | Pays for idle time between bursts | Pays only for actual invocations — cheap |
| Steady, high volume | Fixed cost regardless of utilization | Per-invocation cost paid on every request — can exceed a VM's flat rate |

**How to decide:** below a workload-specific utilization threshold, serverless wins on cost; above it, the per-invocation premium adds up to more than a comparably-sized always-on server would cost.

Long-running or steady high-throughput workloads are where containers or VMs consistently win economically and operationally. A service handling constant, predictable volume all day gets no benefit from scale-to-zero — it never reaches zero — and pays the per-invocation premium on effectively every request.

The same applies to genuinely long-running work — a streaming data processor, a persistent WebSocket server — which serverless's execution time limits and stateless model actively fight against, rather than support.

FaaS goes beyond typical cloud lock-in: your function code is often written against a provider-specific event format, deployed through provider-specific tooling, and wired to provider-specific triggers — a particular queue service, a particular storage event schema. Migrating to another provider isn't a redeploy — it's a partial rewrite of the integration layer.

This isn't necessarily a reason to avoid serverless, but it's a real cost to weigh: the deeper you integrate with provider-specific triggers and services, the more expensive a future migration becomes.

Traditional debugging assumes a long-lived process you can attach a profiler to, inspect memory on, or watch accumulate state over time. A serverless function has none of that — each invocation may run on a different, short-lived instance, so there's no single process to attach to.

Effective serverless observability leans entirely on structured logs, distributed tracing across the trigger chain, and metrics emitted per invocation — debugging shifts from "attach and inspect" to "reconstruct from the trail a request left behind."

slides.subTitle: Modeling the cost crossover point
slides.markdown:
A function costs a small fee per million invocations plus a per-GB-second execution charge. A comparable small VM costs a flat $30/month. Modeling the crossover: at roughly 5 million requests/month with 200ms average execution, the serverless cost approaches and then exceeds the VM's flat $30 — past that volume, the always-on VM is cheaper, and below it, serverless wins by a wide margin.

The exact crossover point depends on execution time and memory per invocation, but the shape is universal: serverless cost scales linearly with volume, a VM's doesn't, so the two lines cross exactly once.

slides.subTitle: Choosing serverless for a workload that never idles
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: serverless is either always cheaper or always more convenient, so it's a safe default. A workload that runs constantly — no idle stretches, steady request volume around the clock — never benefits from scale-to-zero and pays the per-invocation premium on every single request, all day, every day.

The correct model: run the crossover math for the workload's actual traffic pattern before choosing. A workload that never idles is exactly the shape serverless pricing is worst at, even though "serverless" often gets reached for by default.
